title: Mercy for the first of sinners
sum: Paul greets Timothy, his "true child in the faith," and reminds him why he was left in Ephesus: to stop certain people from teaching something different, with myths, endless genealogies and confident talk about the law. The goal of the church's instruction is love from a pure heart, a good conscience and sincere faith. The law is good, Paul says, when it is used for what law is for: to restrain the lawbreakers listed in a catalogue that follows the Ten Commandments.

Then Paul turns to himself. He was once a blasphemer and a persecutor, yet mercy was shown to him, so that he could be the first and model case of what the church's saying declares: "Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners." A burst of praise follows, and the chapter ends with a soldier's charge to Timothy and a warning about two men who wrecked their faith.
readings: Read as a letter to a real coworker

Read as Paul's own letter, chapter 1 is urgent and personal: named opponents (1:20), Paul's own past as a persecutor, prophecies Timothy remembers. Paul backs a younger leader who must face older men in a city Paul knows well (Acts 19-20).
Read as a founding document for church leaders

Read as a later letter in Paul's name, the chapter presents Paul as the pattern convert and the guardian of the true teaching, and Timothy as the model leader who receives it. The "trustworthy saying" and the vice list sound like the settled teaching of a second generation.

views.H: Ephesus was a great city of the province of Asia, where Paul had worked for over two years (Acts 19:8-10). The teachers seem to be insiders, perhaps leaders or would-be teachers in house churches, which fits Paul's warning in Acts 20:30.
views.C: The setting (Paul going to Macedonia, Timothy left behind) does not match Acts 19:22 and 20:1-4, which is one reason many scholars think the letter's setting is a literary frame. Those who hold Paul's authorship place it after Acts 28.
views.L: The chapter is built as a ring: the charge to Timothy (1:3-7), the law and the gospel (1:8-11), Paul's testimony (1:12-17), and the charge again (1:18-20). The phrase "missed the mark" (1:6) returns in the last verse of the letter (6:21), framing the whole.
views.J: The teachers want to be "teachers of the law" (1:7), and the answer is a list of the wrongs the law forbids (1:9-10), which many readers see as following the Ten Commandments. The law is not set aside: it is "a good thing" used lawfully, a position close to Romans 7:12.
views.T: Christian tradition has prized 1:15 as a summary of the whole gospel. The vice list, especially 1:10, is cited in today's debates on sexuality and on slavery.

deep.h: The vice list and the Ten Commandments
deep.b:
Many commentators read 1:9-10 against the Ten Commandments. The first six terms (lawless and unruly, ungodly and sinners, unholy and irreverent) would answer to the duties toward God. Then, on this reading, come the commandments of the second table in order: those who kill father or mother (honor your parents), killers (do not murder), those who commit sexual sin and men who lie with males (do not commit adultery), slave dealers (do not steal, since stealing a person was punished by death, Exodus 21:16), liars and people who swear falsely (do not bear false witness). Bengel and Ellicott saw the order of the Decalogue here; Meyer thought Paul followed it "not adhering to it strictly."

Others are not persuaded. The Expositor's Greek Testament points out that when Paul lists the commandments in Romans 13:9 he puts adultery before murder, and the fit is uneven: two terms fall under adultery, and nothing stands for coveting. Either way, the point of the list is that the law aims at real wrongdoing. Teachers who turned it into myths and genealogies had missed its point.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a letter framed by "missing the mark"
deep.b: The rare verb astocheō, "miss the mark," occurs in 1:6 and again in the letter's last verse, 6:21 (and once in 2 Timothy 2:18). In both places of 1 Timothy it describes the same people, who have missed the mark and wandered off. I suggest the writer used it as a deliberate frame: the letter opens and closes with archers who missed, and everything between (prayer, order, care for widows, contentment) is the target. This is my own observation; commentators note the repeated word, but I have not seen it argued as a frame for the whole letter.

echoes: Acts 19:1-41; Acts 20:17-38; Exodus 20:1-17; Romans 7:12; Galatians 1:13; 1 Corinthians 15:9; Luke 19:10; 1 Corinthians 5:5; 2 Timothy 2:17-18

settings.by: Paul, as the letter presents its writer
settings.to: Timothy, Paul's coworker, left in charge at Ephesus; through him the house churches of Ephesus, who would hear the letter read aloud
settings.when: After Paul has gone on to Macedonia (1:3); on the traditional view, between a release from Roman custody and a second arrest, in the early or middle 60s
settings.why: The greeting sets out Paul's authority ("by the command of God") and names Timothy as his true child, so that the church hears Timothy's orders as Paul's. Knowing the letter would be read aloud explains why a private letter has such public weight.
views: Paul writes to the real Timothy, whom he has left in Ephesus, to back his authority against particular teachers.
A follower of Paul writes in his name late in the first century or early in the second, using Paul and Timothy as the model of a leader handing on sound teaching to the churches of his own day.

settings.what: The charge to stop the other teaching
settings.to: Timothy, and through him the teachers and house churches of Ephesus
settings.when: Paul has gone on to Macedonia and left Timothy behind to deal with teachers in the church
settings.why: To give Timothy the authority to silence teachers who mixed the law with myths and speculation. Paul names the goal of all teaching, love, and shows the law's true use, so that the church would not be pulled into endless debate.
views: Jewish-Christian teachers using the law for speculation (1:7; Titus 1:14), early Gnostic thinkers (6:20), or ascetics (4:3): the letter's hints fit a mix.

settings.to: Timothy and the church at Ephesus
settings.when: In the middle of the charge, as Paul remembers his own call
settings.why: To show what sound teaching produces: a persecutor turned apostle by mercy. Paul's story becomes a pattern for every believer and an answer to teachers who traded the gospel for speculation.

settings.when: Recalling the prophecies made at the start of Timothy's ministry
settings.why: To strengthen Timothy for a hard task by reminding him of his calling, and to warn the church by two named examples, Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom Paul has put out of the fellowship.

title: One God, one mediator
sum: The church gathered for prayer is to pray for every person, kings included, so that believers can live calm and quiet lives. The reason is God himself: he wants everyone to be saved, and there is one God and one mediator, the human Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all. That is why Paul was sent to the Gentiles.

Then come instructions for the gathering: men are to pray without anger or quarreling, and women are to dress modestly and adorn themselves with good works. A woman is to learn in quietness; she is not to teach or hold authority over a man, because Adam was shaped first and Eve was deceived. Yet she will be saved through the bearing of children. These verses (2:11-15) are among the most debated in the Bible.
readings: Read as a lasting order for the church

On this reading, 2:12 gives a rule for every church in every age: the teaching and governing office belongs to qualified men. Its ground is creation (2:13), not a local problem, and 3:1-7 then describes the overseer as a husband and father. This is the view of the Catholic and Orthodox churches on ordination and of complementarian Protestants.
Read as a rule for a church under attack

On this reading, the instructions answer a crisis: false teaching spread from house to house among women (5:13; 2 Timothy 3:6-7) who had not been taught. Paul's first command is that women learn (2:11); the creation story is an illustration, and Eve is a warning about deception. This is the view of egalitarian Christians and of churches that ordain women.

views.H: Ephesus had a famous temple of Artemis, and some have built a theory that the city's religion was led by women and shaped the false teaching (the Kroegers, 1992). S. M. Baugh (1994) answered that the evidence does not show such a culture. Sandra Glahn (2023) argues instead that Artemis was the virgin helper of women in childbirth, which could explain 2:15.
views.C: For critical scholars, 2:11-15 is one of the clearest signs that the Pastorals belong to a later generation, when households and order had become the church's defense against false teaching, and when the freedom of women in Paul's churches (Romans 16; 1 Corinthians 11:5) was being limited. Others see continuity with 1 Corinthians 14:34-35.
views.L: Prayer and quietness frame the chapter: a "calm and quiet" life (2:2) and a woman who learns "in quietness" (2:11-12) share one Greek root. The argument moves from the one God to the one mediator to the one apostle to the Gentiles, then to the men and women of the gathering.
views.J: The appeal to Genesis 2-3 follows Jewish ways of reading Scripture, where the order of a story carries meaning. Praying for rulers (2:2) follows Jeremiah's word to the exiles (Jeremiah 29:7). The one God (2:5) is the Shema of Deuteronomy 6:4.
views.T: 2:4 is central to the debate on election (Augustine, Calvin, Wesley). 2:5 is cited in the debate on the saints' prayers and on Mary (Lumen Gentium 60; Augsburg Confession 21). 2:11-15 is cited in every church's teaching on women in ministry.

deep.b: Five questions decide how a reader takes the passage. (1) Quietness: does hēsychia mean silence, or a calm, teachable manner, the same quiet asked of everyone in 2:2? (2) Authority: does authentein mean to exercise authority in a neutral sense, or to domineer or seize it? (See the note at 2:12.) (3) Teaching: are "teach" and "hold authority" two things, or one ("teach in a domineering way")? (4) The reason: is 2:13-14 a timeless ground (creation order) or an illustration suited to women deceived by false teachers? (5) The scope: was the rule for public worship only, for husbands and wives, or for all teaching? Each church's answer comes from how it answers these. The note on 2:15 gives the five readings of "saved through the bearing of children."

deep.title: Claude's theory: the quiet life for everyone
deep.b: The Greek word for "quiet" in 2:2, hēsychios, and the word for "quietness" in 2:11 and 2:12, hēsychia, share a root, and the chapter begins with the quiet life asked of the whole church. I suggest that 2:11-12 applies that general call to a particular group: women who, the letter says, were being drawn into "empty talk" (1:6) and going from house to house (5:13). On this reading, the quietness asked of women is first of all the quietness asked of every believer, the opposite of the false teachers' noisy debates. The link between 2:2 and 2:11 is noted by many commentators; the suggestion that the letter means them as one call is my own, and it does not by itself settle how far 2:12 reaches.

echoes: Jeremiah 29:7; Deuteronomy 6:4; Mark 10:45; Genesis 2:7; Genesis 2:22; Genesis 3:13; Genesis 3:15-16; 2 Corinthians 11:3; 1 Corinthians 14:34-35; 1 Corinthians 11:3-12; 1 Peter 3:1-6; Romans 5:12

settings.to: The house churches of Ephesus, through Timothy
settings.when: As Timothy sets the church's worship in order
settings.why: To widen the church's prayer to every person, rulers included. Against teachers who may have thought salvation was for a select few, Paul grounds the prayer in God's will to save all and in the one mediator, and he names his own mission to the Gentiles as proof.

settings.what: Men and women in the gathering
settings.to: The men and women of the Ephesian house churches, through Timothy
settings.when: In the same instructions for worship; the church is troubled by teachers who forbid marriage (4:3) and by false teaching spreading in households (5:13)
settings.why: To restore order and peace to the gathering: men are to pray without anger, women to dress modestly and to learn quietly, and women are not to teach or hold authority over men. How far the rule reaches is the question.
views: The reason given is creation, so the rule binds the church's teaching and governing office in every age.
The rule answers a local crisis of false teaching among women not yet taught; once women learn, the reason falls away.
A rule for husbands and wives
Some read gynē and anēr as "wife" and "husband," so the verse governs a wife's relation to her husband in the gathering.

traditions.q: Does God want every person to be saved (2:4), and if so, why are not all saved?
views: "If it is true that no one can save himself, it is also true that God 'desires all men to be saved'" (Catechism 1058, citing this verse), and "the Church prays that no one should be lost." "God predestines no one to go to hell"; for that, a willful turning away from God and persistence in it until the end are necessary (Catechism 1037).

The Confession of Dositheus (1672) teaches that God predestined to glory those he chose and condemned those he rejected, but not without cause, since God "would have all men to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the truth" (citing this verse); he foreknew who would make a right or a wrong use of free will (Decree 3). Chrysostom: when some are lost, it is "because they would not: but His part was done" (Homilies on 1 Timothy 7).

The Formula of Concord (1577) teaches that election "extends only over the godly, beloved children of God," yet God "is in earnest" that all should come to him; it rejects the teaching that "God is unwilling that every one should be saved," and says that not God or his election but people's own wickedness is responsible when they are lost (Epitome, article 11).

The Westminster Confession teaches that by God's decree "some men and angels are predestinated unto everlasting life; and others foreordained to everlasting death" (3.3), the rest being passed by and ordained to dishonor and wrath "for their sin" (3.7). Following Augustine, who took "all men" as "every sort of men" (Enchiridion 103), Calvin wrote that the verse "relates to classes of men, and not to individual persons": no rank or nation is shut out.
Wesley's note: "Who willeth seriously all men - Not a part only, much less the smallest part." God's saving will reaches every person, and people "are not compelled."

The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article V) calls election "the gracious purpose of God, according to which He regenerates, justifies, sanctifies, and glorifies sinners," and says it "is consistent with the free agency of man."

traditions.q: If Christ is the "one mediator" (2:5), may Christians ask the saints and Mary to pray for them?
views: Christ is the one Mediator (Lumen Gentium 60, citing this verse). Mary's motherly role "in no wise obscures or diminishes this unique mediation of Christ"; it draws all its power from it, and her titles such as Mediatrix "neither take away from nor add anything to" Christ's dignity (Lumen Gentium 62).

The Confession of Dositheus (1672) confesses Christ "to be the only mediator," who in "giving Himself a ransom for all" reconciled God and humanity; "notwithstanding, in [our] prayers and supplications unto Him, we say the Saints are intercessors, and, above all, the undefiled Mother of the very God the Word" (Decree 8). Chrysostom reads 2:5 as a statement about who Christ is: "a mediator ought to have communion with both parties" (Homilies on 1 Timothy 7).

The saints may be remembered and imitated, but "the Scriptures do not teach that we are to call on the saints or to ask the saints for help," since Scripture sets before us "the one Christ as the Mediator, Atoning Sacrifice, High Priest, and Intercessor" (Augsburg Confession 21, citing 1 Timothy 2:5-6). The Apology grants that, as they prayed for the church while alive, "so in heaven they pray for the Church in general" (Apology 21.9), but denies that they are to be called upon.

Worship is to be given to God alone, "not to angels, saints, or any other creature: and, since the fall, not without a Mediator; nor in the mediation of any other but of Christ alone" (Westminster Confession 21.2).

The Second London Baptist Confession (1689) uses the same words: worship is given "not to angels, saints, or any other creatures," and "nor in the mediation of any other but Christ alone," citing this verse (22.2).

traditions.q: Does 2:11-15 forbid women to teach or lead in the church today?
views: "Only a baptized man (vir) validly receives sacred ordination" (Catechism 1577, which cites 1 Timothy 3:1-13 among its texts); "for this reason the ordination of women is not possible."

The Orthodox Church in America answers that "the Orthodox Church precludes the ordination of women to the priesthood and episcopacy": "It is a matter of Holy Tradition, as well as a vision of ministry as something not limited to the ordained priesthood." Chrysostom read 2:11-12 as setting women in "the station of learners" in the assembly (Homilies on 1 Timothy 9).

Divided. The Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod does not ordain women; its Commission on Theology and Church Relations report Women in the Church (1985) grounds the apostle's teaching in the order of creation, "not the 'curse' of the fall." The Lutheran Church in America ordained its first woman pastor, Elizabeth Platz, in 1970, and its successor, the ELCA, ordains women.

Divided. Calvin held that the office of teaching is one "which God has committed to men only," and that "extraordinary acts done by God do not overturn the ordinary rules of government," as in Deborah's case. The Presbyterian Church in America keeps the offices of elder and deacon "open to men only" (Book of Church Order 7-2). The Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.) ordains women; it dates its women ministers from Margaret Towner, ordained on October 24, 1956.

Divided by province. The Church of England ordained its first women priests at Bristol Cathedral on 12 March 1994 and consecrated its first woman bishop, Libby Lane, in 2015; from 1993 it also provided "flying bishops" for churches that did not accept the ordination of women.

Wesley's note glossed "To usurp authority over the man" as "By public teaching," yet on 2:13-14 he wrote that woman was "originally the inferior" and "more easily deceived." The Methodist Church in the United States granted full clergy rights to women at its General Conference on May 4, 1956.

The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article VI): "While both men and women are gifted for service in the church, the office of pastor/elder/overseer is limited to men as qualified by Scripture," citing 1 Timothy 2:9-14. This is the Southern Baptist Convention's confession; other Baptist bodies decide the question for themselves and are not shown here.

Women have served in credentialed ministry in the Assemblies of God "since the founding of the Fellowship in 1914." George P. Wood, writing for the denomination, reads 2:11-15 against false teaching at Ephesus and takes authentein as "to assume or usurp authority," so that women may teach without seizing authority.

Divided across churches, in statements made by groups rather than churches. The Danvers Statement (1987) cites 2:11-15 for its view that "some governing and teaching roles within the church are restricted to men." The statement of Christians for Biblical Equality counts 1 Timothy 2:9-15 among "the few isolated texts that appear to restrict the full redemptive freedom of women," which "must not be interpreted simplistically and in contradiction to the rest of Scripture."

title: The household of God
sum: Paul lists what the church should look for in its overseers and its deacons. Overseers must be beyond reproach: the husband of one wife, sober, sensible, hospitable, able to teach, gentle, free from the love of money, good leaders of their own households, not new converts, and well thought of by outsiders. Deacons must be serious and honest, tested first, holding the mystery of the faith with a clean conscience. "Women likewise" are named in the middle of the deacons' list.

Paul then says why he is writing: so that, if he is delayed, Timothy will know how people should live in God's household, "the church of the living God, a pillar and a firm base for the truth." The chapter closes with six lines of an early hymn to Christ: made visible in the flesh, proven right in the Spirit, seen by angels, heralded among the nations, believed in the world, taken up in glory.

views.H: The lists are mostly about character and reputation, much like the lists of virtues in Greek moral writing. They ask for leaders whom outsiders would respect, in a city where the church was small and watched.
views.C: Critical scholars see in these chapters a church with settled offices, a stage later than Paul's lifetime; Titus 1:5-9 has a close parallel. Others answer that Philippians 1:1 already names "overseers and deacons" and Acts 14:23 has elders appointed on Paul's first journey.
views.L: The chapter moves from offices (3:1-13) to the purpose of the whole letter (3:14-15) to the confession that sums up its faith (3:16): order in the church serves the mystery of godliness.
views.J: Elders and overseers had models in the synagogue, which was led by elders and a ruler of the synagogue. The household image (3:15) recalls Moses, "faithful in all my house" (Numbers 12:7; Hebrews 3:2-6).
views.T: These verses are the charter of church office in every tradition: the threefold order of bishops, priests and deacons; the Presbyterian elders; the Baptist pastors and deacons. 3:2 is cited in the debates on married clergy and remarriage, 3:11 on women deacons, 3:15 on the authority of the church, and 3:16 in the history of the Greek text.

deep.b: The six lines are each a verb in the passive voice with a short phrase, and many scholars arrange them in three pairs that alternate between earth and heaven: flesh and Spirit, angels and nations, world and glory. It is not in time order (the Ascension comes last, after the preaching to the nations), which suggests a hymn about Christ's whole work rather than a timeline. It begins with "who," like the hymns in Philippians 2:6 and Colossians 1:15, so it seems to be quoted from the middle of a longer text. The later reading "God was made visible" (KJV "God was manifest") is set out in the variant.

deep.h: Overseers and deacons in 1 Timothy and Titus
deep.b: Titus 1:5-9 gives a list for elders and overseers on Crete that closely parallels 3:1-7: blameless, husband of one wife, not given to wine, not violent, not greedy for gain, hospitable, self-controlled, holding to the teaching. Titus adds that the elder's children must be believers and stresses holding firmly to the message; 1 Timothy adds that the overseer must not be a new convert and must be well thought of by outsiders, fitting an older church in a large city. Titus has no list for deacons.

echoes: Titus 1:5-9; Acts 20:17; Acts 20:28; Philippians 1:1; Romans 16:1-2; Acts 6:1-6; Ephesians 2:19-22; Philippians 2:6-11; Colossians 1:15-20; Acts 1:2; John 1:14

settings.to: Timothy, who must choose or test leaders, and the Ephesian churches who will receive them
settings.when: While false teachers are active, some perhaps among the leaders
settings.why: To give Timothy a standard for choosing and judging leaders, so that the church is led by people of proven character who can teach sound doctrine and whom outsiders respect. The list binds those who choose leaders as much as the leaders themselves.
views: Most churches treat the list as a standard for leaders in every age; they differ on whether "husband of one wife" rules out the unmarried, the remarried or the divorced (see the note).

settings.what: The qualifications of deacons, and of "women likewise"
settings.when: In the same instructions on church leaders
settings.why: To make sure that those who serve the church's practical needs, including its money, are honest, tested and sound in faith.
views: 3:11 gives rules for the wives of deacons (KJV).
3:11 names women who served as deacons, like Phoebe (Romans 16:1).

settings.what: Why Paul writes, and an early hymn
settings.by: Paul, quoting a hymn or confession of the church
settings.when: As Paul hopes to come soon but fears delay
settings.why: To show that all these instructions serve one end: the church, God's household, holding up the truth about Christ, which the hymn sums up.

traditions.q: Overseers (3:1-7) and elders (5:17): are bishops a separate order above elders, and who governs the church?
views: "Bishops by divine institution have succeeded to the place of the apostles"; "by Episcopal consecration the fullness of the sacrament of Orders is conferred" (Lumen Gentium 20-21). The ministry is "exercised on different levels by those who from antiquity have been called bishops, priests and deacons" (Lumen Gentium 28).

"The Holy Spirit has appointed Bishops as leaders and shepherds over particular Churches"; "the dignity of the Episcopate differs from that of the simple Priest," for "the Priest is ordained by the Bishop, but a Bishop is not ordained by a Priest" (Confession of Dositheus, Decree 10).

"It is evident unto all men, diligently reading Holy Scripture and ancient Authors, that from the Apostles' time there have been these Orders of Ministers in Christ's Church,--Bishops, Priests, and Deacons" (Preface to the Ordinal; American Prayer Book of 1928).

The power to preach and forgive "by divine right is common to all who preside over churches"; "it is by human authority that the grades of bishop and elder or pastor are distinct," so "ordination administered by a pastor in his own church is valid by divine law" (Treatise on the Power and Primacy of the Pope, 61-65, citing Jerome and Titus 1:5).

Presbyterian order: the titles bishop, pastor, presbyter, elder and teacher "do not indicate different grades of office, but all describe one and the same office"; within it are "teaching elders and ruling elders," who govern jointly in church courts (Presbyterian Church in America, Book of Church Order 8-1, 7-2, 1-5).

Congregational order: "Its two scriptural offices are that of pastor/elder/overseer and deacon," and "each congregation operates under the Lordship of Christ through democratic processes" (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article VI). The Second London Confession (1689) names the officers "bishops or elders, and deacons," chosen "by the common suffrage of the church itself" (26.8-9).

traditions.q: What does "the husband of one wife" (3:2) mean for married, celibate and remarried clergy? (Baptist teaching is not shown on this card.)
views: Ordained ministers of the Latin Church, except permanent deacons, are normally chosen from men who live celibate "for the sake of the kingdom of heaven" (Catechism 1579). "In the Eastern Churches a different discipline has been in force for many centuries": married men may be ordained deacons and priests, bishops are chosen from celibates, and in East and West no one may marry after ordination (Catechism 1580).

A married man may be ordained, but both he and his wife must have "been married only one time," whether an earlier marriage ended in divorce or death; a widower may be ordained if he "has not remarried," and he "may not marry after his ordination" (Orthodox Church in America). Chrysostom read 3:2 as "prohibiting his having more than one" wife, not requiring marriage.

"For Paul says, 1 Tim. 3:2, that a bishop should be chosen who is the husband of one wife"; "it is also evident that in the ancient Church priests were married men," and "the priests teach that it is lawful for them to marry wives" (Augsburg Confession 23).

"It is lawful for all sorts of people to marry, who are able with judgment to give their consent" (Westminster Confession 24.3), and vows of "perpetual single life" are called "superstitious and sinful snares" (22.7).
Bishops, priests and deacons are not commanded by God's law to vow single life, and may marry at their own discretion (Thirty-Nine Articles, article 32).
Wesley's note: the phrase "neither means that a bishop must be married, nor that he may not marry a second wife," but warns ministers to stand clear of polygamy and divorce "on slight occasions."

traditions.q: Were the "women" of 3:11 deacons, and may women be deacons today? (Lutheran and Anglican teaching is not shown on this card.)
views: Chrysostom: "He is speaking of those who hold the rank of Deaconesses" (Homilies on 1 Timothy 11). Today the Orthodox Church in America answers that the Church does not ordain women as priests or bishops, and names "the role of deaconesses in the early Church" among the questions that deserve serious discussion.

The diaconate is a degree of the sacrament of Holy Orders, which "only a baptized man (vir) validly receives" (Catechism 1577); since the Second Vatican Council married men may be ordained permanent deacons (Lumen Gentium 29; Catechism 1571).

Divided. The Presbyterian Church in America holds that the offices of elder and deacon "are open to men only" (Book of Church Order 7-2); the Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.) ordains women as deacons, ruling elders and teaching elders.
Wesley read 3:11 of deacons' wives: "faithful in all things - both to God, their husbands, and the poor."
The Baptist Faith and Message (2000) names two offices, "pastor/elder/overseer and deacon," and limits only the first to men (article VI).

traditions.q: The church is "a pillar and a firm base for the truth" (3:15). Does the church's teaching authority stand beside Scripture?
views: "The Church, 'the pillar and bulwark of the truth', faithfully guards 'the faith which was once for all delivered to the saints'" (Catechism 171, citing this verse and Jude 3), handing on the apostles' faith through the generations.

Without one faithful reading of Scripture the Church could not be "holy, the pillar and ground of the truth" (citing this verse); "the witness also of the Catholic Church is, we believe, not of inferior authority to that of the Divine Scriptures" (Confession of Dositheus, Decree 2).

"The prophetic and apostolic Scriptures of the Old and of the New Testament alone" are "the sole rule and standard" by which all teachers are judged, and "the Holy Scriptures alone remain the only judge, rule, and standard" (Formula of Concord, Epitome, Rule and Norm 1, 7).

"The supreme judge by which all controversies of religion are to be determined ... can be no other but the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scripture" (Westminster Confession 1.10), for "the purest churches under heaven are subject both to mixture and error" (25.5).
Wesley's note attaches "pillar and ground" to the mystery that follows: it is "the foundation and support of all the truth taught in his church."

title: Train yourself for godliness
sum: The Spirit has warned that some will turn from the faith, misled by teachers who forbid marriage and order people to keep away from certain foods. Paul answers with creation: everything God made is good, and nothing is to be refused if it is received with thanks, because God's word and prayer make it holy.

Then Paul speaks to Timothy himself. Like an athlete in training, he is to train for godliness, which has a promise for this life and the next. He is to give orders and teach, to let no one despise his youth, to give himself to the reading of Scripture, to urging and teaching, and not to neglect the gift given him when the elders laid hands on him. By keeping watch over himself and his teaching, he will save himself and his hearers.

views.H: The teachers forbade marriage and told people to keep clear of some foods (4:3). In Ephesus the church met in households, and a ban on marriage would have struck at the household, the very shape of the church.
views.C: Scholars who date the letter later compare these teachers with second-century groups that rejected marriage and certain foods, and with the stories of Paul and Thecla, in which Paul's preaching leads a young woman to refuse marriage (MacDonald, 1983).
views.L: The chapter turns from "some" who depart (4:1-5) to "you" (4:6-16), the pattern of the whole letter. Athletic words (train, exercise, toil, struggle) bind the second half together.
views.J: The answer to the ascetics is Genesis 1 and the Jewish habit of blessing God before meals. The reading of Scripture in the gathering (4:13) follows the synagogue.
views.T: 4:1-5 is read by Protestants against obligatory clerical celibacy and fasting rules, and by Catholics and Orthodox as a warning against those who call marriage or food evil, which their own disciplines do not do. 4:14 is a key text for ordination.

echoes: Genesis 1:31; Mark 7:19; Romans 14:14; 1 Corinthians 10:25-26; Colossians 2:16-23; Acts 20:29-30; Acts 13:1-3; Numbers 27:18-23; 2 Timothy 1:6; 1 Corinthians 9:24-27

settings.what: A warning about teachers who forbid marriage and foods
settings.by: Paul, passing on what "the Spirit says"
settings.when: As ascetic teaching is spreading in the church
settings.why: To warn the church that such teaching, however strict and holy it looks, comes from deceiving spirits, and to give believers the answer from creation, so that they can marry and eat with thanks and without guilt.

To show Timothy how to win the argument: not by matching the teachers' speculation, but by training in godliness, a blameless life, the public reading and teaching of Scripture, and faithful use of the gift given at his ordination. It also tells the church that Timothy, though young, has been set apart.

traditions.q: Timothy's gift came "with the laying on of the elders' hands" (4:14). Is ordination a sacrament?
views: Holy Orders is a sacrament. The apostles, "by the imposition of hands ... passed on to their auxiliaries the gift of the Spirit" (Catechism 1556, whose footnote points to 1 Timothy 4:14 and 2 Timothy 1:6-7).

The Priesthood is one of the seven mysteries (Confession of Dositheus, Decree 15). A bishop is a "successor of the Apostles, having received in continued succession by the imposition of hands and the invocation of the All-holy Spirit the grace that is given him," and "the ordinations of all orders and degrees in the Church are proper to him" (Decree 10).

"If ordination is understood as carrying out the ministry of the Word, we are willing to call ordination a Sacrament," and then "neither will we refuse to call the laying on of hands a Sacrament" (Apology of the Augsburg Confession 13.11-12).

Orders is one of five rites that are "not to be counted for Sacraments of the Gospel" in the way Baptism and the Lord's Supper are (Thirty-Nine Articles, article 25); yet the Ordinal admits bishops, priests and deacons "by public Prayer, with Imposition of Hands" (Preface to the Ordinal, 1928 American Prayer Book).

"There be only two sacraments ordained by Christ our Lord in the Gospel; that is to say, baptism, and the Supper of the Lord," and neither may be given except by "a minister of the Word lawfully ordained" (Westminster Confession 27.4).

An elder is "chosen thereunto by the common suffrage of the church itself; and solemnly set apart by fasting and prayer, with imposition of hands of the eldership of the church," citing this verse (Second London Baptist Confession 26.9).

title: Widows and elders
sum: Timothy is to treat the church as a family: older men as fathers, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters. Then come detailed rules for widows. The church is to honor and support widows who are truly alone; families must care for their own widows, which is the first duty of godliness. Widows over sixty with a record of good works may be enrolled on the church's list; younger widows should remarry, so as not to fall into idleness and gossip.

Elders who lead well deserve "double honor," including pay, as Scripture says of the ox and the worker. Charges against an elder need two or three witnesses; elders who keep on sinning are to be corrected publicly. Timothy must not lay hands on anyone too quickly, must keep himself pure, and should take a little wine for his health.

views.H: Widows were among the most vulnerable people in the ancient world. The church's support of them was costly, and the rules sort out who should bear the cost: families first, then the church for those with no one.
views.C: The order of enrolled widows, the paid elders and the procedures for accusations point, for many critical scholars, to a later, more organized church. Others note that Acts 6:1 already shows a church organizing support for widows.
views.L: The chapter is built on the family picture of 3:15 and 5:1-2. "Honor" links the widows (5:3) and the elders (5:17), and "honor" includes money in both places.
views.J: The care of widows comes from the law and the prophets (Deuteronomy 14:29; Isaiah 1:17); the rule of two or three witnesses is Deuteronomy 19:15; and Deuteronomy 25:4 on the ox is read, as in Jewish teaching, from the lesser case to the greater.
views.T: 5:17-18 is cited for paying ministers; 5:17 for Reformed "ruling" and "teaching" elders; 5:22 for care in ordination; 5:23 in the debates on alcohol.

echoes: Deuteronomy 14:29; Deuteronomy 24:17-21; Acts 6:1; James 1:27; Deuteronomy 25:4; 1 Corinthians 9:9; Luke 10:7; Matthew 10:10; Deuteronomy 19:15; Matthew 18:16; 2 Corinthians 13:1; 1 Corinthians 7:39-40

settings.what: How to treat church members of every age
settings.when: As Timothy, a young leader, must correct older members
settings.why: To show Timothy how to correct without harshness: as a son, brother and pure-minded younger man in a family.

settings.what: Rules for the support and enrollment of widows
settings.to: Timothy, the families of the church, the widows themselves and believing women with widows in their households
settings.when: When the church's resources were stretched by the number of widows and some young widows were going from house to house
settings.why: To decide who supports whom: families support their own widows, which is basic godliness; the church supports widows who have no one, and enrolls older widows devoted to prayer and good works; younger widows should remarry. The rules bind families as much as the church, and aim both at care for the needy and at the church's good name.
views: Most churches read the principles as lasting (family first, then the church), and the details (age sixty, the list) as local.

settings.what: The pay, discipline and appointment of elders
settings.to: Timothy, the elders and the Ephesian churches
settings.when: When elders needed support and some had sinned or been accused
settings.why: To protect good elders from unfair charges and to support them financially, while making sure that elders who sin are corrected openly and that new leaders are not appointed in haste.

title: Godliness with contentment
sum: Slaves are to honor their masters so that God's name is not spoken against, and those with believing masters are to serve them all the better. Then Paul returns to the false teachers: proud, sick for arguments, and treating godliness as a way to make money. Godliness is indeed great gain, but only with contentment, for we brought nothing into the world. Those who want to be rich fall into a trap, and the love of money is a root of every kind of evil.

Timothy, the "man of God," is to run from these things and pursue righteousness, faith and love, to compete in the good contest of the faith and keep the command until the appearing of the Lord Jesus Christ. A great doxology praises the only Ruler, King of kings, who alone is immortal. The rich are told to hope in God and be rich in good works. Last of all, Timothy must guard what was entrusted to him and avoid "knowledge" that is falsely named.

views.H: The church had slaves and wealthy members side by side. Teachers who charged for their teaching were common in Greek cities. Pontius Pilate (6:13) ties the faith to a real time in history.
views.C: "The knowledge that wrongly bears that name" (6:20) and "counterclaims" (antitheseis) have led some scholars to date the letter to the second century, against the Gnostics or Marcion's book the Antitheses. Others find the words natural in Paul's day.
views.L: The chapter mirrors chapter 1: false teachers, a charge to Timothy, a doxology, a last warning. Wealth runs through it: gain (6:5-6), the rich (6:9-10, 17-19), and the deposit to guard (6:20).
views.J: "Man of God" (6:11) is the title of Moses and the prophets. The doxology (6:15-16) is built from Jewish praise: the God of gods and Lord of lords (Deuteronomy 10:17), whom no one can see and live (Exodus 33:20).
views.T: 6:10 is among the most quoted and misquoted verses of the Bible. 6:1-2 was argued over in the slavery debates. 6:20 shaped the church's language for guarding the "deposit of faith."

echoes: Ephesians 6:5-9; Colossians 3:22-4:1; Philemon 16; Job 1:21; Ecclesiastes 5:15; Luke 12:16-21; Hebrews 13:5; John 18:37; Deuteronomy 10:17; Revelation 17:14; Revelation 19:16; Exodus 33:20; 2 Timothy 1:12-14

settings.to: Christian slaves in the Ephesian churches, some with pagan masters and some with believing masters
settings.when: In a church where slaves and masters worshiped together
settings.why: To protect the church's witness: slaves who despised their masters, or took advantage of believing masters as "brothers," would bring the name of God and the teaching into contempt. The letter does not address the institution of slavery itself.
views: Defenders of slavery in the 1800s cited such texts; opponents answered from the whole of Scripture, including 1:10 (slave dealers) and Philemon 16.

settings.what: The false teachers and the love of money
settings.when: As teachers seek gain from their teaching
settings.why: To expose the teachers' motives and to warn the whole church that the desire for wealth leads away from the faith.

settings.what: The charge to the man of God, and a doxology
settings.when: Recalling Timothy's confession before many witnesses
settings.why: To call Timothy to the opposite life, of pursuit and contest rather than gain, under the eye of God and of Christ, who made his own confession before Pilate.

settings.to: The wealthy members of the Ephesian churches, through Timothy
settings.when: In a church whose patrons were wealthy
settings.why: To turn wealth into generosity: the rich are not told to give up everything, but to put their hope in God and to be rich in good works.

settings.to: Timothy, and in the plural blessing the whole church
settings.when: At the close of the letter
settings.why: To sum up the letter in one command: guard what has been entrusted, and avoid the falsely named knowledge.
